title: Towards an integrated approach to evaluating biodiversity‐ and water‐sensitive urban design: A review of popular software tools
content:
Globally, cities are recognising a need to design for biodiversity and water together—though current approaches typically design for them independently. Our review of 39 Water and Biodiversity Sensitive Urban Design (BSUD & WSUD) software-based tools identified obstacles to collaboration associated with integration and interoperability. Obstacles included: differences in spatial and tabular data compatibility, financial barriers to licensing and barriers to training resources. We highlight key avenues for tool development to promote integration and interoperability between WSUD and BSUD associated with the accessibility and flexibility of tools. These include lower licensing costs, more beginner training tutorials, case study examples using custom-integrated code, tools with open-source accessibility, GIS compatibility and multi-format interoperability.


Abstract

Globally, cities are recognising a need to incorporate blue-green infrastructure and ecosystem-based approaches into urban design and development. With this recognition comes the need to design for biodiversity and water together—though current approaches typically consider these systems independently. The consequences of this are that relationships between biodiversity and water are overlooked, leading to a reduction in system resilience and functionality. We propose that one challenge to integrating Water and Biodiversity Sensitive Urban Design (WSUD & BSUD) is a lack of compatible analytical tools to enable collaboration and/or integration. We reviewed and analysed attributes of accessibility, interoperability and compatibility for integration in 39 potential WSUD and BSUD software tools. We found a lower financial barrier for accessibility to BSUD tools; and while few BSUD or WSUD tools were operable by a novice, more WSUD tools required a high level of training. BSUD tools were more adaptable to cross-platform use (e.g. Windows/Mac/cloud-based data) and use with GIS-based programs. BSUD tools also had more spatial inputs and outputs compared to WSUD tools, which may explain obstacles to interoperability and collaboration. For better interoperability and collaboration, reviewed BSUD tools should develop more tabular inputs and outputs and WSUD, more spatial inputs and outputs. Fewer WSUD tools were open-source, limiting opportunities for pre-existing software tools to be ‘bridged’ with software architecture, or thoroughly integrated into a single novel tool. Increasing the number of training tutorials, lowering cost licensing, open-source access and multi-format interoperability in software tools are likely to increase the opportunities for integration or collaboration between BSUD ecologists and WSUD hydrologists. Better still would be the development of software packages that are specifically designed to measure both BSUD and WSUD. Practical implication: There are clear practical applications for integrating BSUD & WSUD, including the delivery and efficiency of synergistic benefits and improved management of trade-offs between biodiversity- and water-related outcomes.
